items.title: A coin doesn't 'owe' you a head after 10 tails — but a casino does
items.claim: 10 tails in a row. Probability of the next flip being heads is still 1/2. The coin has no memory. Casinos exploit the gambler's fallacy — players betting against 'streaks' actually have no edge.
items.prompt: Why doesn't the law of large numbers help short-term?

options.text: The law of large numbers only applies to dice

LLN guarantees long-run frequency convergence to expected probability, but does NOT mean short-term deviations must be 'corrected' by reverse outcomes. Each flip is independent: past results carry no information
Tails must come back to balance heads

items.reveal_title: Gambler's fallacy and the law of large numbers (correctly stated)
items.reveal:
Gambler's fallacy: the false belief that, in a sequence of independent random events, recent 'streaks' make the opposite outcome more likely.

Monte Carlo Casino, 1913: black came up 26 times in a row at a roulette table. Players reportedly lost millions betting on red, believing the streak 'must' end. Each spin was independent; the probability of red on the 27th spin was the same as on the first (~18/37 for a European wheel, less than 1/2 because of the green zero).

LLN says: as n increases, the SAMPLE PROPORTION approaches the TRUE PROBABILITY. After 10 tails in a row out of 10 flips, the proportion is 100% tails. After a million more fair flips (with roughly 500,000 each side), the cumulative proportion approaches 50%. But this happens by SWAMPING the early streak, not by REVERSING it. The next flip after 10 tails is still 50/50.

Inverse mistake (hot-hand fallacy): assuming streaks WILL continue (sports). Actually mixed evidence — some sports skills appear to genuinely streak (basketball shooting under some studies), others don't. Distinguishing real streaks from spurious ones requires careful statistics.

Gambler's fallacy explains casino profits even when individual games are 'fair-ish'. House edges (~5% in roulette) compound over many bets; players betting against streaks don't gain anything.

The broader cognitive pattern: humans expect randomness to be uniform. Real randomness has clusters and streaks. Mistaking real randomness for 'patterns' is one of the most consistently studied errors in cognitive psychology.
items.why: Past results feel like they should influence future probabilities. They don't, for independent events. Misunderstanding this drives gambling losses, conspiracy theories, and bad predictions across domains.

items.title: Your average speed never equals your speed at most moments
items.claim: Drive 60 miles in one hour at varying speeds — slowing for lights, accelerating onto highways. Average speed is 60 mph. But that doesn't mean you were doing 60 mph for most of the time. You may have spent more time at 30 mph than at 90 mph.
items.prompt: What's the difference between average and instantaneous?

options.text: Average and instantaneous are equal at the midpoint

Average speed = total distance / total time. Instantaneous speed = the limit of average speed over a vanishing interval — the derivative dx/dt. The mean value theorem guarantees at SOME instant the instantaneous speed equals the average, but not at most or all instants

items.reveal:
Mean Value Theorem (MVT): if f is continuous on [a, b] and differentiable on (a, b), then there exists c in (a, b) such that f'(c) = (f(b) - f(a)) / (b - a).

In driving terms: at SOME moment during your journey, your instantaneous speed was exactly equal to your average speed. (Not all moments — at least one.) This is the rigorous version of what intuition gets right.

Applications:
- Speed cameras using 'average speed enforcement': measure entry and exit times over a stretch; if average exceeds limit, you must have exceeded the limit at SOME moment (MVT). This is legally watertight.
- Optimisation: locating extrema where f'(c) = 0.
- L'Hopital's rule and Taylor's theorem are MVT consequences.

The full Taylor expansion exploits this: f(b) = f(a) + f'(a)(b-a) + (1/2)f''(a)(b-a)^2 + ... Each term corrects the linear approximation with higher-order behaviour. The remainder terms involve derivatives at intermediate points (Lagrange remainder).

Derivative as instantaneous rate: dx/dt at t = t_0 is the limit as h approaches 0 of (x(t_0 + h) - x(t_0)) / h. Defined when this limit exists. It tells you the rate of change exactly at time t_0 — not over any finite interval.

Velocity (vector) vs speed (scalar magnitude). At a U-turn, average velocity over the round trip is zero (you end up back where you started), but average speed is non-zero. Distinguishing them is key in kinematics.
items.why: Average rates feel like reliable summaries of what happened. The mean value theorem guarantees only ONE instant matches the average; for most of a journey, instantaneous speed differs. Speed limits use both.

items.title: 20% of people own 80% of the wealth — and 4% own 64%
items.claim: Vilfredo Pareto observed in 1896 that ~20% of Italians owned ~80% of the land. The pattern recurs in income, book sales, software bugs, city sizes, earthquake magnitudes. Apply 80/20 again to that 20%: 4% own 64%. And again: 0.8% own 51.2%.
items.prompt: Why is this 'fractal' inequality so common?

options.text: Many natural and social processes follow POWER LAWS: P(X > x) is proportional to x to some negative power. Power-law distributions exhibit self-similarity at all scales, including the recursive 80/20 split
It is true only for exactly 20%

items.reveal:
A power-law distribution: the probability that a quantity exceeds x is proportional to x^(-alpha), for some exponent alpha. The Pareto distribution is the canonical example.

When alpha is in a particular range (specifically when the exponent gives an 80/20 split), the distribution is 'self-similar': the top 20% has 80% of the total; within that top 20%, the top 20% (i.e., the top 4%) holds 80% of THEIR share (i.e., 64% of the whole).

Key examples:
- US household wealth: top 20% own ~85%; top 1% own ~32%.
- Earthquakes: each unit increase in magnitude is ~10x less frequent.
- City sizes (Zipf's law, also power law).
- Web site visits, book sales, file sizes, software bug counts.
- Word frequencies in language (Zipf).

Generative mechanisms: 'rich-get-richer' (preferential attachment, scale-free networks — Barabási, Albert 1999); multiplicative growth; minimax processes.

Power laws contrast with normal distributions (bell curves) where extreme values are vanishingly rare. In power-law distributions, extreme values dominate — and you can't reason about averages as 'typical'.
items.why: Equality intuitions assume bell curves. Many real distributions are power laws — where the top few items dwarf the rest, and inequality is built into the math.
